WATCH: After calling Putin his friend, Trump 'can't speak to' whether Putin is a friend to America
Politics
Updated on Nov 20, 2026 4:32 PM EST — Published on
Nov 20, 2026 2:09 PM EST
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump doubled down Friday on his description of Vladimir Putin as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether the Russian president is a friend to the U.S.
Watch the video in the player above.
Trump also insisted during a White House news conference that Putin wants peace with Ukraine, despite Russia's continued aggression after invading more than four years ago. Asked about the most recent attacks — hours after Putin met with Trump in China — Trump suggested that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Putin share equal responsibility for the ongoing conflict.
"He'd love to end the war," the U.S. president said of his Russian counterpart. But, "you have two guys that don't know how to end it. We're trying to help them. You have two people that hate each other, Zelensky and Putin. They don't know how to end it. They want to end it. They're both stuck in it."
Educate your inbox
Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics
newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
During a wide-ranging news conference, Trump praised both Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping after returning from China, where he participated in bilateral and trilateral meetings with his fellow heads of state.
Trump raised eyebrows on the trip with his warm welcome and repeated references to Putin as his "friend." He made no effort in the White House briefing room to walk back the comments. And he noticeably sidestepped a specific question about whether he views Putin as a friend to the United States.
"I can't speak to America," Trump said, without expounding.
He shifted immediately to his "very good" personal relationship with Putin and repeated longstanding grievances over the extended federal probe that concluded that Russian agents sought to influence U.S. voters in the 2016 presidential election on Trump's behalf.
Watch the video in the player above.
"I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship (with)," Trump said. "It's actually very good."
"I've been dealing with Putin" since "the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax," as Trump calls the Department of Justice investigation. "It was a hoax made up by the Democrats" and "probably helped me win," Trump said.
Trump insisted his relationships with the other world leaders is key to an eventual peace.
"You know, you're very lucky to have somebody that has a relationship with the heads of the most powerful countries," he said.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who stood on stage during Trump's news conference and made brief remarks, echoed the president's sentiments, pushing back against criticisms that Trump was embracing autocratic leaders as trusted allies.
"I want everybody to understand the relationships between heads of state are invaluable," said Rubio, who traveled with Trump to Asia. "It sets the tone for the entire relationship. It sets the tone for our trade negotiators. It sets the tone for our diplomats."
Barrow reported from Atlanta.

WATCH: Trump on data centers: 'Take advantage, don't shut them off'
Politics
Nov 20, 2026 4:25 PM EST
President Donald Trump says he's not going to allow American companies to build data centers in other countries.
During a briefing at the White House on Friday, Trump said data centers will reduce taxes, lower electricity costs and make "a lot of money" in a pitch for communities to allow them to be constructed.
Watch the video in the player above.
"Make them pay your community, but take advantage," Trump said. "Don't shut them off."
Voters in the recent midterm elections overwhelmingly supported restricting or banning data center development in dozens of state and local ballot measures across the country.
The president said he doesn't want to allow the centers to be built outside the U.S. "because China will take all of them." He added that companies that try to build elsewhere will face "tremendous penalties."
Trump's remarks came a day after he returned from a summit in China with its president, Xi Jinping, and Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
"Whoever wins SI wins," Trump said, referring to "superintelligence," the administration's term for AI.

WATCH: Trump hosts news conference after meeting with Xi, Putin
Politics
Updated on Nov 20, 2026 3:46 PM EST — Published on
Nov 20, 2026 11:59 AM EST
WASHINGTON (AP) — Beijing is building nuclear weapons at a "hot and heavy" pace, President Donald Trump said Friday, a day after he met Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin and the three countries agreed to talks on preventing nuclear proliferation.
Watch the news conference in the player above.
While Russia and the U.S. lead the world by each possessing thousands of nuclear weapons, China is rapidly expanding its nuclear arsenal. In its annual review of China's military buildup, the Pentagon said China's stockpile of nuclear warheads remained in the low 600s through 2024, but the country was on track to have more than 1,000 warheads by 2030.
"They'll catch us within 10 years," Trump said of China's nuclear buildup during a news conference at the White House. "They're going at it hot and heavy, but they have a lot."
WATCH: Inside the historic summit between Trump, Xi and Putin
Trump's public remarks were his first since his controversial summit with Xi and Putin, leaders of countries long considered U.S. rivals, in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen on Thursday. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who spoke to reporters alongside Trump on Friday, said it was imperative for the three nuclear powers to talk.
"These three countries possess the overwhelming majority of nuclear weapons on this planet," Rubio said. "The idea that these three leaders should not engage on a regular basis is not just absurd, it's dangerous."
After the trilateral meeting, the leaders issued a joint statement, saying they "affirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought" and "will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons."
Prior to the meeting, observers had doubted if China would agree to nuclear talks. With a much smaller nuclear arsenal, Beijing had resisted joining nuclear arms control talks with the U.S. and Russia.
-- Didi Tang, Associated Press

Climate talks in overtime as nations wrestle with response to worsening global warming
World
Nov 21, 2026 12:03 PM EST
ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Work crews boxed up the venue for this year's United Nations climate talks in Turkey, as negotiators went into overtime on Saturday in an attempt to reach a final agreement on global warming. But hopes are slim that additional discussions will produce concrete plans to slash fossil fuel use.
The added day of talks came as the two-week annual summit, or COP31, drew strong condemnation for failing to mention fossil fuels in a draft of the final agreement. The document is meant to address how the world will deal with climate change, which drives heat waves, floods and other disasters.
To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts said the world needs to urgently and drastically cut emissions from the use of coal, oil and gas.
READ MORE: Activists, leaders criticize COP31 climate talks as fossil fuels go unmentioned in draft deal
In a letter sent on Saturday to this year's co-hosts, Turkey and Australia, 100 civil society groups warned that they were "on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs" the U.N. has ever held. The letter stated there were only hours left "to save this COP from becoming a low point of three decades of climate negotiations."
In the lead-up to these talks, the U.N. announced that the world will likely blow past the 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.
"No one knows what is happening behind closed doors, or what the outcome of COP31 will be," said Teresa Anderson, global lead on climate justice at ActionAid International.
Climate talks enter overtime
Inside an area of the COP31 venue known as the pavilions, where countries showcased innovations and hosted panels, workers were seen packing up electronics and boxing up belongings on Saturday.
The hallways, previously bustling with tens of thousands of participants, stood largely empty, with only a handful of security guards seen taking photos by deserted pavilions.
"COP31 is in a bleak overtime, with dwindling food and water, and no sign of any progress since the alarmingly underwhelming texts we saw earlier," said Rachel Cleetus of the Union of Concerned Scientists, who is at the venue in the Mediterranean coastal city of Antalya.
Earlier during the summit, the nonprofit Climate Action Tracker warned that progress on slowing global warming has stalled for the past five years, even as disasters — including this year's heat waves in Europe and flooding in Nepal — become more deadly.
READ MORE: UN chief says 'immediate and drastic' emissions cuts needed to avert climate change catastrophe
Countries most vulnerable to climate change, including small island nations whose lands are battered by rising seas, also say wealthy nations that caused the climate crisis must contribute more to U.N. funds to help them recover from disasters and adapt to a warmer world.
"Every year there seems to be a greater discontent, a mistrust and frustration for civil society, indigenous people and countries that are more climate vulnerable," said Tuvalu's Minister of Environment Maina Talia, during a Saturday press conference.
"I am still holding the line, trying to be very optimistic until we see the text," he said.
The United States, a major polluter and the world's largest economy, did not participate directly in this year's talks.
The next climate summit will take place in Ethiopia's capital, Addis Ababa, in November 2027.
Criticism of COP31 grows
On Friday, a protester wearing a red noose around his neck and a vest emblazoned with the slogan "you are killing the future" interrupted official proceedings by clambering onto a table and shouting: "You take out fossil fuels. You killed 1.5. There is no money. Just kill me now. The Global South cannot wait."
The Global South isn't a geographical term, but a reference to developing countries in general. As the protester was escorted out by security, he shouted: "You keep doing nothing at all. Nothing at all. Kill me now. Kill me now."
READ MORE: At UN climate talks, 5 nations back plan to double rooftop solar panels by 2030
The demonstration interrupted Turkey's Minister of Environment and COP31 co-president Murat Kurum, who said "let's try to maintain the peace in the room" before continuing with his scheduled remarks.
"Yesterday, of course, this place was buzzing and today it's nearly empty. But all the key negotiators are here, civil society is here, watching the negotiations," said Harjeet Singh, a strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, who has attended 18 climate summits.
"We are still stuck with many, many disagreements and nobody knows how long this will go on," he said.
Borenstein reported from Kensington, Maryland, Delgado from Bangkok, Arasu from Bengaluru, India, and Milko from Islamabad, Pakistan. Associated Press journalist Tammy

Texas says an execution went as planned. A witness says screams showed 'tremendous distress'
Nation
Nov 21, 2026 11:46 AM EST
A Texas official on Friday defended how the state carried out the execution of a 70-year-old man who loudly insisted he was in pain and pleaded, "Don't let me suffer like this," during a lethal injection that followed a struggle to find a suitable vein.
Yet Reinaldo Dennes' spiritual adviser, who had his hand on Dennes' shoulder inside the death chamber in Huntsville, said he felt like he was holding a bucking bronco Thursday.
WATCH: Christa Pike describes pain after botched execution
"Twice he said, 'It's not working. It's not working. It's not going how it's supposed to go. This isn't right.' Those types of words kept coming," said the Rev. Jeff Hood, a death penalty opponent.
Dennes was "clearly in tremendous distress," said Hood, who called it torture.
It was the ninth execution this year in Texas, which has a long history of using the death penalty as punishment for murder. Executions across the U.S. have garnered more attention since Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital in Tennessee in September. The drug didn't enter her bloodstream correctly.
State says execution worked 'as planned'
Amanda Hernandez, a spokesperson for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice, said initial attempts to place two IV lines into Dennes' hands and arms were unsuccessful.
Dennes was strapped to the gurney at 6:04 p.m. Hernandez said an IV was successfully placed in the left side of his neck 16 minutes later at 6:20 p.m., followed by another line in his left foot at 6:38 p.m.
Witnesses, including Hood and an Associated Press reporter, were escorted into the death chamber before Dennes began his final statement at 6:52 p.m. Lethal drugs began flowing less than a minute later, Hernandez said.
Almost immediately, Dennes exclaimed: "The pain! Go! Go!" He uttered an expletive and implored "the father" to "take this pain."
He subsequently shouted: "My right leg is killing me!" and described it as a cramp. After another profanity, he grunted, then said, "I don't think this is normal. Take me, father. Don't let me suffer like this. C'mon."
READ MORE: Alabama executes man for 1991 killings in last of 3 U.S. executions carried out the same day
The drugs were stopped at 7:07 p.m., and he was declared dead a minute later, slightly more than an hour after he was restrained in the death chamber, Hernandez said.
"We feel that all of our processes and procedures were followed and that it was carried out as planned," she told the AP.
Hernandez said she didn't know how many attempts were made to place IV lines.
"It's not a race — it's not how quickly can we get this done," she said. "It's something you want to do correctly. There is no normal time limit. It's what it takes for it to be successfully done."
In May, Tennessee called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers after failing for over an hour to establish an IV line. Idaho, in 2024, tried eight times to establish a line to execute Thomas Creech before stopping. Republican Gov. Brad Little subsequently signed a law making a firing squad the primary method of execution.
Advocate says Dennes would not fake pain
As for Dennes' claims of extreme pain, Hernandez said the state plans no additional inquiry. She said there were reasons to suspect he was exaggerating, adding that he complained even before the lethal drugs were given and grumbled about pain in a leg that didn't have an IV line.
Hernandez said "it makes you wonder" if the high-profile Pike case has influenced death row inmates to act out.
"They watch the news. He was aware of the other executions," Hernandez said.
Dr. Paul Wax, executive director of the American College of Medical Toxicology, said he couldn't think of any reason why an injection of pentobarbital into the left foot or left side of the neck would cause pain in the right leg.
Michael Graczyk, The AP reporter who attended the execution, said witnesses can't see when the drug starts to be administered. Dennes' foot was covered by a sheet, and the IV in the left side of his neck wasn't visible from their position.
READ MORE: IV team warned Christa Pike's vein might have 'blown' during failed execution, court filing says
It's not possible to definitively know what caused him to scream in pain. Hernandez said the lethal drugs had not passed their expiration date, though she didn't know the date.
Hood, the spiritual adviser, said assertions that Dennes was faking pain were "disgusting."
"We have heard them say repeatedly since last night that this was not botched. That is absolutely, unbelievably absurd," Hood said.
Dale Baich, an Arizona lawyer who has represented death row inmates and witnessed 17 U.S. executions, said the latest Texas lethal injection raises concerns.
"Calling a prisoner's screams an act is not a medical finding. It is an accusation, and the state should be required to produce evidence to support it," Baich said.
Associated Press reporter Kate Brumback in Atlanta contributed to this story.

Bessent says no further restrictions are needed for Nvidia chip exports to China
Politics
Nov 21, 2026 11:28 AM EST
WASHINGTON (AP) — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday that no further restrictions on the sale of older Nvidia chips to China are needed following the Trump administration's move earlier this week to block China's remote access to the latest semiconductors.
The ability of Chinese tech firms to access Nvidia's technology came under scrutiny after CEO Jensen Huang stepped down amid allegations of his affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that uses advanced chips to generate computing power that Chinese firms access remotely.
"The proper chip restrictions are in place," Bessent said in an interview with CNBC after returning from a trip to Asia with President Donald Trump. "And the remote access has been curtailed."
WATCH: Bessent accuses Lutnick of failing to prevent China from obtaining Nvidia chips
Bessent's comments came a day after the House Foreign Affairs Committee released details of the Commerce Department's approval of the sales of more than 850,000 chips from Nvidia and its competitor AMD to Chinese companies. The Pentagon has identified some of those companies as having ties to the Chinese military.
The report tracked applications from Nvidia to sell its H200 chips — one of its more powerful products, though not the most advanced — and AMD's applications to sell its roughly comparable MI325X chip to companies that are either located or headquartered in China, or entities with parent companies based in China.
Educate your inbox
Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics
newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else.
The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security approved the export, re-export, or transfer of 879,868 of these chips to companies with Chinese ties across 21 license applications as of May 11, 2026, the report said. Nvidia and AMD had requested to sell a cumulative total of more than 3.4 million of the chips to Chinese-tied companies across those applications, per the report.
The approvals, which don't necessarily indicate completed sales, included 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent and its subsidiaries, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD, according to the report. Each of those companies has been identified by the Defense Department as having ties to the Chinese military.
The report shows the Commerce Department has a "long track record of transparency with Congress about licensing activity for the H200 and equivalent chips, including both approvals and rejections," a spokesperson for the Bureau of Industry and Security said in a statement Friday.
The spokesperson said the Commerce Department's approach to H200 licensing is based on a rule in the Federal Register that was published in January. The rule imposes "significant additional national security-related requirements on license applicants in order to qualify for case-by-case consideration rather than a presumption of denial," the spokesperson said.
An Nvidia spokesperson said in a statement Friday that the "limited shipments we made under the H200 program were legal and authorized" by the BIS. "The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes," the company spokesperson said.
WATCH: Trump says he would love former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to 'be given a second chance'
Earlier this week, Nvidia said it was no longer shipping H200 chips to China. The spokesperson said Friday that shipments had stopped despite prior approvals.
AMD said it complies with U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains "rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations" in a statement from a spokesperson Friday. "We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity," the spokesperson said.
Chinese technology firms have been bracing for impacts on their ambitious AI development plans as scrutiny mounts on export controls in the U.S.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been under intense scrutiny himself in the wake of the turmoil following the Huang affair. Last week, Bessent said he was frustrated with the Commerce Department's delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to Megaspeed International, which is under investigation by the U.S. for potentially diverting restricted Nvidia AI chips to China. A former executive at the company who allegedly had an affair with Huang was reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being a spy for China.
In an unusually public rebuke of a fellow Cabinet member, Bessent said his department wanted to place export controls on Megaspeed, but Commerce was in charge of the matter.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Trump said he has "not lost confidence" in Lutnick. Calling him a "different kind of guy," Trump said he "has a natural business instinct" and has "done a very good job."
Huamani reported from Los Angeles. Associated Press writer Meg Kinnard contributed from Columbia, South Carolina.

Rights groups urge sanctions after ICJ finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
World
Nov 20, 2026 7:28 PM EST
UNITED NATIONS (AP) — Rights groups are calling for military and economic sanctions against Myanmar after the United Nations' highest court, in the first ruling of its kind, determined that its government committed genocide against the Rohingya minority in a brutal 2017 military operation.
WATCH: International Court of Justice finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
The International Court of Justice has no power to enforce Thursday's ruling, which orders Myanmar's military-supported government to allow those who fled the violence to return home safely, to pay reparations to the Rohingya Muslims and prosecute those suspected of having committed genocide.
Myanmar's government has denied committing genocide, claiming it acted against insurgents, and is considered unlikely to fulfill any of the court's demands. President Min Aung Hlaing, the former military leader, was in charge of the 2017 operation. The court said evidence showed Myanmar forces killed about 100,000 Rohingya.
Khine Khine Soe, the president's spokeswoman, noted the International Court of Justice decision handed down Thursday had been the result of a nine-to-six vote of the judges.
"Not all 15 judges agreed with the decision," she told reporters in the capital Naypyitaw. "So it was not a decision made unanimously. I would say that it was unfair."
While the World Court's rulings are final and legally binding, it has no recourse beyond reporting noncompliance to the U.N. Security Council.
UN Security Council has the power to impose sanctions
The Security Council scheduled closed consultations on the ruling next Wednesday and a private meeting on Dec. 7 at the request of the United Kingdom, which expelled Myanmar's defense attache after Thursday's ruling.
But Daniel Forti, the International Crisis Group's head of U.N. affairs, said it's unlikely there will be any immediate action from the 15-member Security Council, which could impose sanctions on Myanmar. He said any action would likely be blocked by China and Russia, both permanent members with veto power.
"China has discouraged the Security Council from acting on the Myanmar file since 2021, as it is reluctant to cede any influence in its own backyard," Forti told The Associated Press. "The ICJ ruling will not alter China's calculations, and it is hard to imagine that either Beijing or Moscow would support any potential Security Council resolution that attempts to enforce the court's recommendations."
READ MORE: Myanmar is the first state found responsible for genocide. Here's how the ICJ ruled in other cases
Forti said Gambia, which launched the court proceedings, may eventually pursue a resolution in the 193-member General Assembly calling on Myanmar to comply with the ICJ's demands, even though its actions are not legally binding, unlike those of the Security Council.
General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman plans to hold "an informal dialogue" with the U.N.'s 193 member nations on the ICJ ruling and remains open to other exchanges, assembly spokesperson Melissa Summers said. Rahman, who is also Bangladesh's foreign minister, went to Cox's Bazaar Friday and told a crowd of Rohingya "at this historic moment" that there must be action and pledged to be their voice in New York, she said.
Justice for All, an American human rights organization that advocates for the rights of Muslim minorities, called on the Trump administration to support a General Assembly resolution demanding Myanmar's compliance with the judgment, and establishing international monitoring and follow-up.
Rights groups call for targeting Myanmar's economy and military
Justice for All, which has a task force of 38 U.S. and Canadian Muslim organizations that have advocated for Rohingya rights since 2017, argued that sanctions should target Myanmar's oil and gas sector and the networks that provide weapons and other support to its military.
Amnesty International's Secretary General Agnes Callamard urged governments not to welcome the president "on the international stage, especially as grave violations continue unchecked inside Myanmar."
"Instead, they should stop any transfer of all weapons, security and surveillance equipment, and military and security assistance to Myanmar," she said. "The U.N. Security Council should impose a global arms embargo and refer the entire situation in Myanmar to the International Criminal Court."
That court, however, is under U.S. sanctions along with many of its judges and staff, so any action by the Security Council would face an almost certain U.S. veto.
Prosecutors at the ICC requested an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing in late 2024 alleging he was responsible for crimes against humanity against the Rohingya. There has been no public announcement on a decision by judges at the court who would have to issue a warrant.

Federal jury convicts man of starting deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
Nation
Nov 20, 2026 7:01 PM EST
LOS ANGELES (AP) — The man accused of sparking last year's deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges Friday after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.
READ MORE: Mistrial declared after jury deadlocks in arson trial over deadly 2025 Palisades Fire in Los Angeles
Jurors convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.
Rinderknecht, with little apparent reaction, gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. His father was present for the trial and as the verdict was read.
Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.
Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht's first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial.
During the second trial, prosecutors presented a more tightly organized case that presented digital forensic data, expert testimony and Rinderknecht's state of mind in the hours leading up to the fire. They did not focus as much on his resentment toward the rich and powerful to present the crime as arson motivated by "societal revenge" like they previously did.
Prosecutors zeroed in on evidence placing him at the fire's origin area, such as photographs that showed his car parked at the base of a trail leading up to where the fire started and cellphone tower data pointing to his movement on the hill. Fire detection camera images showed the time window the blaze ignited, and experts eliminated any other source of ignition that night, including fireworks.
They established that Rinderknecht was acting erratic and angry in the hours leading up to the fire through the testimony of Uber passengers and texts sent to his girlfriend at the time.
"He was mad at everything, and frustrated," said Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams.
After the fire began, Rinderknecht called 911 more than a dozen times as he walked down the hill. Prosecutors presented the video he screen-recorded on his phone while calling. As he was calling, he asked ChatGPT: "Are you at fault if a fire is lit because of your cigarettes?"
These were part of an alibi Rinderknecht was trying to create for himself, prosecutors said.
They also presented extensive testimony on how fire investigators determined the Palisades Fire was a holdover fire from the initial blaze Rinderknecht sparked. Jurors were instructed not to consider the Los Angeles Fire Department's role in putting out the fire.
Rinderknecht's defense attorney Steve Haney casted doubt on the government's case and said that their evidence proves nothing.
Haney said the fire scene could have been compromised because the area was accessible to the public until the Palisades Fire started Jan. 7.
"Six days of anyone and everyone walking across the spot the government now calls a crime scene," he said.
The defense called their own expert witnesses, including a retired fire investigator for the U.S. Forest Service who argued the fire origin area was different from what the government concluded.
Haney argued the government could not conclusively say there was no one else by the fire ignition point that night because of missing cell data records, and pointed to a neighbor's testimony that he saw a group of teenagers running away from the direction of the trailhead.
He told jurors to disregard any evidence related to Rinderknecht's character, such as his angry text messages, because they were "evidence of the man, not evidence of the act."
Finally, Haney presented an alternate explanation for what ignited the fire — fireworks. Multiple witnesses, including two neighbors and a local firefighter, all said they heard a loud bang or explosion from the direction of the hill the fire purportedly started on.
In the thousands of images of the evening collected from cameras in the area, none showed fireworks in the sky above the hill where the fire started, prosecutors said.
